claims.text: Section 8006(a), DoD Appropriations Act 2026: the tables in the classified annex accompanying the Act are 'hereby required by law to be carried out in the manner provided by such tables to the same extent as if the tables were included in the text of this Act.'

Section 4001(d), NDAA FY2026: 'Applicability to Classified Annex.--This section applies to any classified annex that accompanies this Act', where section 4001(a) authorises obligation and expenditure of any dollar amount specified in a funding table.

Section 8059, DoD Appropriations Act 2026, directs a continuing classified quarterly report to the Appropriations Defense subcommittees 'on certain matters as directed in the classified annex accompanying this Act.'

Section 5 of the NDAA FY2026 gives the joint explanatory statement printed in the Congressional Record on or about 10 December 2025 the same effect as a conference committee joint explanatory statement.

The classified annex is the single mechanism by which an activity can be simultaneously funded by law and absent from every public document, because the statutory text incorporates it by reference without reproducing it. Reasoning: section 8006(a) equates the annex tables to statutory text; no publication requirement attaches to the annex; therefore an appropriation with full legal force exists that has no public expression at any level of detail.

desc: Every year Congress enacts two sets of numbers for the Department of Defense. One is printed in the United States Statutes at Large and can be read by anyone. The other is the classified annex, and it has been given, by express statutory text, exactly the same legal force. Section 8006(a) of the Department of Defense Appropriations Act for fiscal year 2026 (division of Public Law 119-75, approved 3 February 2026) provides that with regard to the programme, project and activity tables in the explanatory statement 'and the tables contained in the classified annex accompanying this Act, the obligation and expenditure of amounts appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act for those programs, projects, and activities are hereby required by law to be carried out in the manner provided by such tables to the same extent as if the tables were included in the text of this Act.' The authorisation side does the same thing: section 4001(d) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (Public Law 119-60, approved 18 December 2025) states simply 'Applicability to Classified Annex.--This section applies to any classified annex that accompanies this Act', section 4001(a) having just provided that a dollar amount in a funding table is thereby authorised for obligation and expenditure. The annex is prepared by the four defense committees, is not printed in the Congressional Record, is not available to members who are not on the relevant committees without arrangement, and is never published. Its contents are the programme-element-level detail for classified activity: the actual line items, the actual dollar figures, the actual programme names. Section 8059 of the FY2026 appropriations act directs the Secretary of Defense to continue providing 'a classified quarterly report ... on certain matters as directed in the classified annex accompanying this Act' - the annex is thus itself the source of reporting requirements whose subject matter is unknown to the public. This is the structure that answers the question posed at the top of this board: money reaches a programme that does not appear as a budget line because the budget line exists, is legally binding, and is in a document nobody outside a small circle has read.

claims.text: Congress attaches classified addenda to three annual national security acts -- the Intelligence Authorization Act, the National Defense Authorization Act, and the Department of Defense Appropriations Act -- and no addendum has ever been published, even in redacted form.

Over 36 years Congress wrote at least 124 provisions in 68 Public Laws that can reasonably be read to give classified addenda legal force; about half were full or partial incorporation provisions. Counting committee reports, Congress has produced at least 271 reports with classified addenda since 1977.

Virtually all annual Intelligence Authorization Acts stipulate at Section 102 that funding authorizations and personnel levels "are those specified in the classified Schedule of Authorizations," and accompanying report language states that the classified Schedule "is incorporated by reference in the Act and has the legal status of public law."

Congress has used annex-incorporation provisions to earmark specific sums invisibly, including $4.8 billion for "classified programs, described...in the classified annex" at the height of the Iraq war.

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) permits the Secretary of Defense to waive any requirement under subsections (a), (b) or (c) that certain information be included in a special access program report if the Secretary determines that inclusion "would adversely affect the national security," on a case-by-case basis.

When the Secretary of Defense exercises the 10 U.S.C. 119(e) waiver, the withheld information and the waiver justification go only "jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees" -- twelve members of Congress.

Section 1673 of the FY2023 NDAA (50 U.S.C. 3373b), drafted with input from David Grusch while he was in government, created the 72-hour tripwire for programs not reported to the defense or intelligence committees -- the direct legislative counterpart to grusch-misappropriation-allegation.

dossier.denialPosture: There is no denial to catalogue here, because the mechanism is openly documented in statute and doctrine and defended on its merits: the Intelligence Community's chief lawyer has publicly agreed that classified schedules carry the legal status of public law. The concealment is not denied; it is legislated.
dossier.narrative:
The classified annex is the least glamorous object on this board and the most important. It is the mechanism that makes the rest of the question -- who, where, under what authority, paid for how -- answerable in principle and unanswerable in practice.

Dakota Rudesill, a former Senate Budget Committee staffer and Intelligence Community official, published the only serious empirical study of the practice. His finding: over thirty-six years Congress wrote at least 124 provisions in 68 Public Laws that can reasonably be read to give classified addenda the force of law, and produced at least 271 committee reports carrying classified addenda since 1977. About half of the 124 were incorporation provisions -- statutory text whose entire operative content is a pointer to a document nobody outside the compartment will ever see. The standard formulation appears at Section 102 of virtually every Intelligence Authorization Act: the amounts authorized and the personnel ceilings "are those specified in the classified Schedule of Authorizations." Accompanying report language routinely states that the Schedule "is incorporated by reference in the Act and has the legal status of public law." The Intelligence Community's own top lawyer has agreed with that characterization.

Rudesill is careful, and his carefulness is itself evidence. He notes that nothing is publicly known about the length of any annex -- "An individual addendum could be two pages long, or 20, or 200" -- and that each committee invites members to read the addenda in a secure room, but "few do." He also records that the practice accelerated: Congress wrote more force-of-law annex provisions in 2011-2015 than in the first eight Congresses of the practice combined, from 1977 to 1992. This is the shape of a mechanism that grew because it worked.

The second layer is statutory rather than procedural. 10 U.S.C. 119 is the SAP oversight statute. Subsection (a) requires an annual March 1 report to the six defense committees listing every DoD special access program, with descriptions, milestones, actual costs by year, and estimated costs across a six-year horizon. Subsection (b) requires a February 1 notice and justification for every new SAP. Subsection (f) forbids initiating a SAP until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse. On its face this is real oversight.

Subsection (e) is the escape hatch. The Secretary of Defense "may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report" upon determining that inclusion "would adversely affect the national security." When he does, the information and the justification go "jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees" -- twelve members of Congress, no staff specified. DoD Instruction 5205.11 builds the corresponding category into doctrine: a waived SAP is "An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs."

The third layer is the one almost nobody has noticed. The U.S. Code note appended to Section 119 reads: "For termination, effective Dec. 31, 2021, of provisions in subsecs. (a) and (b) of this section requiring submittal of annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328." The annual SAP report and the new-SAP notice -- the two provisions that produced a written, dated, comprehensive inventory of the black budget's program structure -- were swept away by a generic reporting-burden sunset enacted in the FY2017 NDAA. The subsection (e) waiver survives; the reports it was designed to abridge do not.

Against that background, Congress in December 2022 legislated a tell. 50 U.S.C. 3373b(a)(4)(B) -- Section 1673 of the FY2023 NDAA -- requires the Secretary of Defense, within 72 hours, to report to the defense and intelligence committees and to congressional leadership any authorized UAP disclosure that relates to "a restricted access activity, a special access program, or a compartmented access program that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to the congressional defense committees or the congressional intelligence committees." Congress does not write 72-hour tripwires for hypotheticals. The statute is a signed, dated legislative acknowledgment that unreported access programs are a live possibility.

AARO has since conceded, in its own words, one instance: "In 2021, without sufficient justification, the scope of an IC Controlled Access Program was expanded to protect UAP reverse-engineering." AARO adds that the program never recovered or reverse-engineered anything and was disestablished for lack of merit. Set aside the exculpatory half. The admitted half is that a controlled access program was expanded without sufficient justification, in 2021, specifically to protect UAP reverse-engineering -- which is precisely the nesting behavior Grusch described when he said agencies were "nesting UAP activities in conventional SAP/CAP programs ... without appropriate reporting to various oversight authorities."

Finally, the annex logic reappears in the disclosure statute itself. Under Section 1843 of the FY2024 NDAA, a UAP record may be withheld from the National Archives collection when "the original classification authority makes a determination that there is clear and convincing evidence" of enumerated harms. The original classification authority is the agency holding the record. The annex principle -- the withholder judges the withholding -- survived into the law written to end it.
openQuestions: Whether any classified annex from 1944 to the present contains a line item, program identifier or nickname corresponding to a materials-retrieval or exploitation effort -- no annex has ever been released.
Which specific SAPs, if any, have had 10 U.S.C. 119(e) waivers applied to them, and how many waivers have been issued in total; the statute requires no public accounting.
Whether the December 31, 2021 termination of the 119(a) and 119(b) reporting requirements was substantively debated or was a drafting artifact of a generic reporting-burden sunset.
Whether the DoD or IC has ever complied with the 72-hour notification requirement of 50 U.S.C. 3373b(a)(4)(B), and how many such notifications have been made.
The identity of the IC Controlled Access Program whose scope AARO says was expanded in 2021 'without sufficient justification' to protect UAP reverse-engineering, and who authorized the expansion.
dossier.whatItIs: The classified addenda -- variously called annexes, schedules, appendices and supplements -- attached to the three annual national security statutes (Intelligence Authorization Act, National Defense Authorization Act, Department of Defense Appropriations Act) and to the committee reports that accompany them. Together with the classified notification channels of 10 U.S.C. 119, they are the legal machinery by which Congress appropriates money and issues binding direction to programs whose existence is not public. No classified annex has ever been published, in any form, redacted or otherwise.
dossier.whyImplicated: If a legacy retrieval and reverse-engineering effort has been funded for eight decades, the money moved through this channel, because there is no other channel that both carries the force of law and never surfaces. The annex system is not a leak in oversight; it is a purpose-built container that gives classified direction "the legal status of public law" while keeping it in a safe in a secure room that few members ever enter. Layered on top of it, 10 U.S.C. 119(e) lets the Secretary of Defense strip specified content out of the Special Access Program reports entirely and deliver it to only twelve people -- the chair and ranking member of six bodies. And the statutory backbone that forced annual SAP disclosure at all, 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and (b), was terminated effective December 31, 2021 by a sunset provision Congress itself enacted. David Grusch's sworn answer to the funding question -- "misappropriation of funds and self-fund" -- describes an abuse that this architecture is uniquely well designed to conceal, because the annex records what Congress intended to buy but the public record cannot be reconciled against it.
